semantic_correction.stem: During a 2-month well-child visit, the nurse gives the birth parent a validated postpartum depression screening tool. Which explanation best describes why this screening is part of pediatric preventive care?

options.A: It gives repeated opportunities to identify a birth parent who may need further evaluation and support, helping protect both the parent and the infant.
options.B: It lets the pediatric team diagnose postpartum depression from the screening score alone and begin psychiatric treatment without another assessment.
options.C: It is reserved for visits when feeding, growth, or development concerns suggest that the birth parent may already be experiencing depression.
options.D: It is primarily a one-time check at the 2-month visit because later routine screening is unnecessary when the initial result is negative.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current Bright Futures/AAP preventive-care guidance includes maternal depression screening during the 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-child visits, and AAP guidance explains that repeated screening creates additional opportunities to identify postpartum depression, support the parent-infant dyad, and arrange further evaluation or referral when indicated. B is incorrect because a positive screening result indicates risk and requires further assessment; screening alone is not diagnostic. C is incorrect because screening is routine preventive care at specified early well-child visits rather than being limited to visits where infant problems are already present. D is incorrect because AAP guidance recommends repeated screening through the 6-month well-child visit rather than a single 2-month screen.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Explain that postpartum depression screening is repeated during early well-child care to identify birth parents who may need further assessment and support, thereby supporting both the parent and the infant; a positive screen is not itself a diagnosis.
semantic_correction.source_document_title: Preventive Care/Periodicity Schedule; Incorporating Recognition and Management of Perinatal Depression Into Pediatric Practice
semantic_correction.source_version_date: Bright Futures/AAP Periodicity Schedule current 2025 schedule (updated February 7, 2025 with no clinical-guidance changes); AAP Clinical Report, Pediatrics 2019; current official pages accessed August 21, 2026
semantic_correction.source_locator: AAP Preventive Care/Periodicity Schedule — Maternal Depression Screening: screening at the 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month visits. AAP Clinical Report — Recommendations: integrate routine postpartum depression screening at 1, 2, 4, and 6 months using a validated tool; screening discussion: repeated screening maximizes opportunities to identify affected parents and engage the parent-infant dyad; a positive screen indicates risk and screening is not diagnostic, so further assessment/referral is required when indicated.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: AAP recommends validated postpartum depression screening at the 1-, 2-, 4-, and 6-month well-child visits; repeated screening supports identification, further assessment/referral, and the parent-infant dyad, while a positive screen does not establish a diagnosis by itself.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests the preventive purpose of repeated postpartum-depression screening with one clearly best answer and no correct-option length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It accurately states the purpose of repeated screening: identify risk, prompt further evaluation/support, and support the parent-infant dyad.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. AAP explicitly states that screening is not diagnostic; a positive result requires further assessment and appropriate referral or treatment planning.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. AAP recommends routine screening at specified well-child visits, not only when infant problems suggest possible parental depression.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Current AAP preventive guidance recommends screening at 1, 2, 4, and 6 months, so a negative 2-month screen does not eliminate later routine screening.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A alone explains the preventive rationale for repeated screening; B misuses a screening tool diagnostically, C incorrectly makes screening symptom-triggered, and D contradicts the recommended repeated schedule.
cueing_check: All four choices are explanatory statements of comparable length (A 151, B 148, C 141, D 137 characters). No option is uniquely detailed, absolute, or structurally privileged enough to cue the correct response.
